value.overview: The Bare-crowned Antbird (Gymnocichla nudiceps) is a shy, ground-foraging antbird of humid tropical forests in Central America and northern South America. It is the only species in the genus Gymnocichla. The species is often found in dense understory, forest edges, second-growth vegetation, and overgrown plantations. It frequently follows army-ant swarms, catching insects and other small animals flushed into view by the moving ants.
value.classification: The Bare-crowned Antbird belongs to the antbird family Thamnophilidae and the subfamily Thamnophilinae. Gymnocichla is a monotypic genus, containing only this species.
value.identification: The male is mainly black, with conspicuous white wing markings and bright blue, featherless skin on the forehead, crown, lores, and around the eyes. The female is generally rusty or olive-brown, with a bright blue bare eyering and less contrasting wing markings. It is a medium-sized, short-tailed antbird with a stout bill. It usually stays low in thick vegetation and may be detected first by its clear, accelerating series of whistles or sharp calls.
value.rangeHabitat: The Bare-crowned Antbird occurs from southern Mexico and Belize through Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, continuing into northern Colombia. In Costa Rica it is found on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, but is absent or very scarce in the dry northwest; records include humid lowlands and foothills, with occurrences reaching roughly 1,200 meters. It favors evergreen forest edges, dense secondary growth, regenerating clearings, overgrown plantations, swampy ground, and vegetation beside streams.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident rather than a regular migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals are present throughout the year on suitable Caribbean- and Pacific-slope habitat, with no reliable evidence of seasonal passage or long-distance migration.
value.breeding: The breeding biology of this species remains poorly known, but documented nests in Costa Rica show a small domed structure made from fine plant fibers, dead leaves, and palm material. Nests have been placed very close to the ground in dense understory vegetation, including on horizontal Philodendron stems and broken palms. Clutches of two white eggs marked with brown blotches have been reported. Both parents participate in incubation, brooding, and feeding the nestlings, which receive spiders and small insect larvae.
value.dietFeeding: The Bare-crowned Antbird feeds mainly on insects and other arthropods, including beetles, cockroaches, ants, grasshoppers, spiders, and small insect larvae. It may also take small lizards. Foraging occurs singly, in pairs, or in family groups, usually on the ground or within about 2.5 meters of it. The bird hops through dense vegetation, gleaning prey from leaves and branches and making short lunges or jumps to capture prey.
value.behavior: This antbird is usually quiet, elusive, and closely associated with dense understory. It often occurs in pairs and may accompany army-ant swarms, taking prey that flee from the ants. Away from swarms it generally associates less often with mixed-species flocks. Individuals may bob or vibrate the tail while calling or singing. Their low-level movements, dark plumage in males, and preference for tangled vegetation can make them difficult to observe even where they are locally regular.
